If you are on UNIX, then use

unix.time(for(i in 1:1000) results[i,1:3] <- FUN())

More sophisticated:

sttime <- proc.time()         ## note start time
for (i in 1:m){               ## loop over repeated sampling experiments

  y <- beta[1] + beta[2]*x + rnorm(n=length(x),
                                   sd=sigma)  ## manufacture data
  bols[i,] <- coef(lm(y~x))               ## ols, store estimates
  blms[i,] <- coef(lqs(y~x,method="lms")) ## least median squares
  ttime <- (proc.time()-sttime)[3]
  atime <- ttime/i
  cat(paste("Sampling experiment",i,"done:",
            round(ttime,2),
            "seconds elapsed",
            round(atime,3),
            "average\n"))    ## message to user
}                            ## close loop

messages.body_plain:
INFORMATION ON S-NEWS

Please save this information for future reference, especially to
modify your subscription or unsubscribe in the future.

The full introduction message contains additional information on the
following topics.

1. S-news objectives and appropriate use.
2. S-news addresses and subscriptions.
3. To unsubscribe...
4. Replying to messages on S-news.
5. General guidelines for posting to S-news.
6. S-news archives.
7. Mail exploders.
8. Who maintains the s-news list?
9. What should I do if I have questions or comments about list policies or
        management?  (The "s-news-advisory" list.)
10. Features of the Washington University list server.
11. Important list management commands.

To obtain the full message, send a message to

           s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu

containing the single line in the BODY of the message:

           intro s-news

or point your Web browser at:

           http://www.biostat.wustl.edu/s-news/s-news-intro.html
-----------------------------------------------------------

TO UNSUBSCRIBE

Use one of the following forms, sent in the BODY of a
message to
           s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu
referring to the appropriate list (regular delivery or daily digest),
and including the address you are subscribed under only if it is different
from your current mailing address.

                     unsubscribe s-news
                     unsubscribe s-news myname at my.address
                     unsubscribe s-news-digest
                     unsubscribe s-news-digest myname at my.address
-----------------------------------------------------------

S-NEWS OBJECTIVES AND APPROPRIATE USE

S-news is the discussion group on the S and S-plus systems for
statistics, graphics, and programming.  Appropriate topics must be
related to S/S-plus, including programming and usage questions and
suggestions, problem reports, and announcements of new software
(contributed and commercial), books and articles, and conferences and
educational events.  Short job announcements are also acceptable.  Long
advertisements and commercial messages that are not specifically relevant
to S/S-plus are not acceptable.
-----------------------------------------------------------

S-NEWS ADDRESSES

Mail for posting to the S-news list should be sent to:

     s-news at wubios.wustl.edu

All subscription and unsubscription requests and other list management
commands should be sent to

     s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu

Messages that require human intervention should be sent to

     s-news-owner at wubios.wustl.edu

but you should make use of the automatic list processor commands whenever
they cover the situation.
-----------------------------------------------------------

IMPORTANT LIST MANAGEMENT COMMANDS

All Majordomo list management commands should be sent to
s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu.  The command (or multiple commands)
should be in the body of the message, not in the subject line.  If your
mailer puts a signature at the end of the message, put the command
           end
after your list commands so the signature is not interpreted as
commands.  NEVER send commands to s-news!  (NEVER!)

A full list of Majordomo commands can be obtained by sending the command
           help

To subscribe to the list, send the command
           subscribe s-news
or for the digest version,
           subscribe s-news-digest
You will be sent a confirmation message to which you must reply to make
sure that you actually desired to subscribe.  This is intended to prevent
forged subscriptions.  Note that subscriptions to the immediate-delivery
and digest versions are handled like two separate lists, so if you want to
switch from immediate delivery to digest, you must unsubscribe to s-news
and subscribe to s-news-digest.

If you want to subscribe using a different address than the one you are
sending from, use the command
           subscribe s-news myname at my.address

To unsubscribe, send one of the following commands as appropriate:
           unsubscribe s-news
           unsubscribe s-news-digest
           unsubscribe s-news myname at my.address
           unsubscribe s-news-digest myname at my.address

messages.subject: [S] piper diagrams
messages.body_plain:
In response to a question on piper diagrams, I am sending a short
explanation
of the plot and a pdf file with a picture of a piper diagram.

The short explanation==================================
A piper diagram is a form of the trilinear diagram. The piper diagram has
two simple triangular plots on the right and left side of a 4-sided center
field.

In the triangular plots, the axes should run from 0 to 100 on each of the
three sides.
In the right triangle, the axes increase in a counter-clockwise
direction--the axis
restarts to zero at each apex; in the left triangle, the axes increase in a
clockwise
direction--restarting at zero at each apex.

For each sample, there are three variables to determine the plotting
position
 in each triangular plot, for example the axes may be the three major
cations (left) and anions (right) and the variables are the cation/anion
composition of the sample. Each of the three cation/anion variables, in
milliequivalents, is divided by the sum of the three values, to produce a
percent of total cations. For example, if Ca= 0.80 meq,
Mg =0.26 meq, and Na+K = 0.89 meq, then %Ca = 41,
%Mg = 13, and %[Na+K} = 46.

The data points in the center field are located by extending the points
in the lower triangles to the point of intersection in the center field.The
axis values at the top and bottom of the center field are 100; the
axis values on the left and right side of the center field are 0.

A pdf file with a picture of a piper diagram====================
(See attached file: piper.pdf)

In the attached piper diagram, the circles that are plotted in the
center field have areas that are proportional to dissolved-solid
concentration.

messages.subject: [S] indexing vector problem
messages.body_plain:
Dear S Users,

I would like to get a logical vector indicating whether or not a row name of a
matrix is contained in a vector of names.  I plan to use the resulting logical
vector to assign missing values to elements of a column in the matrix where the
logical vector is true.  I would like to use something like the following (which
doesn't work)

mymat[dimnames(mymat)[[1]]==names,2]<-NA

where names is a character string vector.  But, this doesn't work with names
being a vector.

So, my inexperience with s+ leads to this ugly work around:

select<-vector(mode="logical", length=nrow(mymat))
for (name in names) select<-(select | (dimnames(mymat)[[1]]==name))
mymat[select,2]<-NA

There must be a better way.  Any suggestions?  Thanks.
-- 
----------

mymat[!match(dimnames(mymat)[[1]], names, 0), 2] <- NA

messages.subject: [S] polar smoothing
messages.body_plain:
As a tangent to the piper diagram question...   and sorry if this has been 
covered already ...

Does anyone know of S+ code for a polar smoother? This is a smoother which 
describes the "centroid"
of a data set, and is created by computing the coordinates of the points in 
polar form and smoothing as a function of angle. When the points are 
re-constituted in x-y space, the result is an "envelope" which surrounds the 
center of the data. Very nice for multi-group data visualization. 

Anyway, this smoothing is commonly used within piper diagrams to lessen the 
"noise" of many data points which may have many symbol types. 

The reference I have is: Cleveland and McGill, "The Many Faces of A Scatter 
Plot", JASA, V 79, Number 388, Dec. 1984. 

I have most of this coded, but (I think) I am stuck at the point where the 
smoothing is done in polar space. The centered (x,y) data are transferred into 
polar coordinates, and then smoothed as a function of theta.  As the authors 
note, the theta are a circular variable, and so a straightforward smoothing 
 (i.e. smooth.fit <- lm(x~y) ) won't work. They suggest to trick a lowess 
routine into performing a circular smooth. This is where I am stuck. 

I though that since the authors were both statisticians at AT&T Bell, and 
probably had some influence on the original S language, that ... well.. you get 
the idea. I will summarize for the group if necessary. 

Thanks all

PS. Virginia - Hi. Good to see other geologists using Splus! Lets stay in touch.

Michael Slattery

I am using S-PLUS2000 (Release 2) under Windows 98.

The following is weird.  It is also very annoying,
as I do generally want numbers of NAs noted when
I do a tabulation on data that has been imported
from a spreadsheet.

I created two data frames that were (almost) identical,
(1) called test1, by importing the data from a spreadsheet,
and (2) called xy, by using data.frame from the
command line.  In both instances the first
column has the numbers
[1]  1  2  3  4  5 NA NA
Yet table(<vector>,exclude = NULL)
gives different results in the two cases.

Does anyone have any light on what may be happening?  

# Create test1 by reading in an Excel file
# NB: Sourcing the data structure below
# gives a test1 that behaves in the same way as xy
# See below for the dump of test1
> table(test1$V1,exclude=NULL)
 1 2 3 4 5 NA 
 1 1 1 1 1  0

> is.factor(test$V1)  # Just checking
[1] F

# Create xy at the command line:
> xy <- data.frame(V1=c(1:5,NA,NA),V2=letters[1:7],
+ V3=c(11,NA,12:15,15))
> table(xy$V1,exclude=NULL)
 1 2 3 4 5 NA 
 1 1 1 1 1  2

Here is what one gets when xy and test1 are dumped:
"xy"<-
structure(.Data = list(V1 = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, NA, NA), 
        V2 = structure(.Data = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),

        .Label = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g"),

        V3 = c(11, NA, 12, 13, 14, 15, 15)), 
        row.names = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7"),

> attributes(test1$V2)
$levels:
[1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" "g"

$levels:
[1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" "g"

> table(v1,exclude=NULL)

messages.subject: [S] GAMs & categorical analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am currently analyzing daily time series data using a GAM framework with
a Poisson link function. I would like to control for a particular
covariate using a categorical predictor having seven unique levels
(independent and in no order of significance). The analysis is further
complicated by the necessity to breakdown the matrix into seasonal
distributions. I am a relatively new user of S-plus and have purchased the
Windows 2000 version. My problem is this - 

The form of the model is:

y ~ a + lo(b) + c (categorical, 1-7) + d

I would ideally like to assess the beta of d in terms of a certain level
of c with a and lo(b) remaining constant. Would it be appropriate to use
the subset option to specify the categorical level of c? Should I create
dummy variables for different levels of c (i.e. if c = 3, then c could
equal 1 or 0 depending on the count of a 3 for a particular observation)?
Or would it be prudent to organize the data according to each category in
c and run regression within each category?

I suppose this is more of a modelling problem. Hopefully I am not
repeating a question that has already been asked. 
Thank you,

Daniel Rainham

University of Alberta

messages.subject: [S] AsIs class
messages.body_plain:
Regarding John Maindonald's query about how table() reports NAs being 
dependent upon how the object was created: the only difference in 
structure I can see is the presense of that bloody "AsIs" class in 
V2. Why this would affect V1 is beyond me; maybe there's some other 
difference not shown in the structure...

In Splus 5.1, if you use importData() with stringsAsFactor=F and then 
look at the class() of character variables, they have class 'AsIs' 
followed by annoying behavior during subsequent use of those 
variables.

For example, suppose I have a tab delimited ascii file like this:
grp     x
a       1
a       2
b       3
b       4

And I import it like this:

tst <- importData('tst.dat','ascii',delim='\t',
                  stringsAsFactors=F)

Then,

> class(tst$grp)
[1] "AsIs"
> unique(tst$grp)
[1] "a" "b"
attr(, "class"):
character(0)
>

Considering that the Splus5.1 Users Guide says about the 
stringsAsFactors argument: "logical flag: if TRUE, strings are 
converted to factors when imported" one might reasonably expect that 
strings would remain strings, in which case the class should be 
'character' or 'string'. But 'AsIs'??? What purpose does this have???

This extra baggage that is being carried along with tst$grp is very 
annoying. I now routinely, manually, convert all elements of class 
'AsIs' to class 'character' after every use of importData().

Notice also that the class 'AsIs' apparently does not exist:
> grep( class(tst$grp) , allClasses() )
numeric(0)

If someone could point me to documentation (if it exists) that 
explains the purpose and function of the class 'AsIs' I would sure 
appreciate it.

-Don

messages.subject_clean: [S] Calculation of z-statistic for spearman's rho
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,

I'm using S+2000, Release 2.  In the function cor.test, when
method="spearman" the z-statistic is computed as

     sqrt(n-1)*coef - (6*sqrt(n-1)/(n^3-n))

where coef is the correlation of the ranks of the X's and Y's.  In all the
textbooks I have the z-statistic is given as simply sqrt(n-1)*coef.  Does
anyone know of a reference that explains why the constant
6*sqrt(n-1)/(n^3-n) is subtracted from the usual z-statistic?

Thanks so much for your time!

Sincerely,

messages.body_plain:
Steven,

My recollection is that an F or t test provides more accurate p-values
than does the normal approximation, and if you use midranks for ties and
use the usual t statistic on the ranks it works well.  You may want to
take a look at the spearman2 function in the Hmisc library, which takes
the approach I've outlined, and generalizes to Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis
tests for categorical X.  It also generalizes to a Spearman test that does not
assume monotonicity in (X,Y).  -Frank

>
> where coef is the correlation of the ranks of the X's and Y's.  In all the
> textbooks I have the z-statistic is given as simply sqrt(n-1)*coef.  Does

messages.subject: [S] Mysterious error message with confint
messages.body_plain:
I have encountered a mysterious error message while using confint.  I post
this message hoping that someone has encountered this problem before and can
explain the nature of the problem.  Here are the steps which led to the
error.

>Par.Init_list(R=R)
>nls.fit_nls(y~E+(I-E)*exp(-(H-L)/R),data=DFnls,
               start=Par.Init,control=list(maxiter=150))
>nls.prof_profile(nls.fit)
>confint(nls.prof)

Error in [: No dim attribute for array subset: c(22.611922791088, ..)

I believe the error occurs in the function "confint.profile.nls" and appears
to be caused by [, pm] in this line:

sp <- spline(x = pro[, "par.vals"][, pm], y = pro$tau)

At the point of the error message, the variables have these values:

pm=1
pro=
          tau par.vals 
 1 -2.7098090 22.61192
 2 -2.1563245 23.47835
 3 -1.6026964 24.38995
 4 -1.0489844 25.34924
 5 -0.4968601 26.35581
 6  0.0000000 27.30628
 7  0.5019421 28.31286
 8  1.0042878 29.36805
 9  1.5063745 30.47333
10  2.0084116 31.63166
11  2.5103966 32.84572
12  3.0123296 34.11831

In the original call to nls, there was only one non-fixed parameter.  My
only guess is that confint is expecting to find at least two random
parameters.

Kevin Wright, Pioneer Hi-Bred Int'l

messages.subject: [S] Multiple axis labels
messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much for all of the input regarding my question about
multiple axis showing on my graphs.  The problem, as stated by Bill Dunlap,
was most definitely the "Create Editable Graphics" option being in the on
position.  The following is his response to my question: 

 Are you using Splus2000?  If so try going to the Options/GraphOptions
 dialog box and unchecking the "Create Editable Graphics" checkbox and
 see if the problem goes away.
 
 That fixed it for me in the follow example:
 
> d <- split(state.x77[,"Frost"], state.region)
> box.pos <- boxplot(d)
> # if you want more lines of tick labels, increase par("mar")[1]
> for(line in 1:3)
>   axis(1, at=box.pos, lab=paste(levels(state.region),line), line=line,
tick=F)

If you want to use the Editable Graphics setting you can change the
axis command to

    mtext(side=1, at=box.pos, text=paste(levels(state.region),line),
line=line+0.5)

and get just the labels.

messages.body_plain:
I think everyone who writes C code to be linked with S-Plus under UNIX would
be interested in the replies I got from Bill Dunlap. Thank you very much,
Bill.

Also it seems like GDB does not understand Sun's CC debug information.

This is Bill's first message:

On Wed, 1 Mar 2000, Vadim Ogranovich wrote:
        > Hi, I am trying to work this out following J. Chambers Green Book
suggestion
        > to attach to the process. I have a strange problem though: the
Splus LIBRARY
        > seems to strip away the debug symbol table from the *.o files it
links. Did
        > anyone manage to link S.so WITH the debug information? Thanks,
Vadim

On Solaris with the SunPro 4 C compiler and dbx you need to edit the
makefile that Splus5 CHAPTER produces and add -g to LOCAL_CFLAGS so the
compiler includes the debugging entries in the compiled code.  I'm not sure
if this would work with gcc.
I tried this in a new directory containing the file a.c:
        % cat a.c
        mycode(double *x, long *n)
        {
        long i ;
        for(i=0;i<*n;i++) {
        *x = *x * *x ;
                }
        }
        % Splus5 CHAPTER a.c
        % Splus5 make S.so

Then I can debug S.so after starting Splus under the debugger with
        % Splus5 dbx 'Splus5 SHOME'/cmd/Sqpe
        Reading symbolic information for Sqpe
        Reading symbolic information for rtld /usr/lib/ld.so.1
        ...
        (dbx) run 
        Running: Sqpe 
        (process id 12792)
        Reading symbolic information for S.so
        S-PLUS : Copyright © 1988, 2000 MathSoft, Inc.
        S : Copyright Lucent Technologies, Inc.
        Version 6.0 Release 1 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.5 : 2000 
        Working data will be in .Data 
                > ^Cdbx: warning: Interrupt ignored but forwarded to child.
        signal INT (Interrupt) in poll at 0xef737874
        poll+0x4:       ta      0x8
        (dbx) stop in mycode
        (2) stop in mycode
        (dbx) cont          
        .C("mycode", 3.0, as.integer(3))[[2]]
        stopped in mycode at line 4 in file "a.c"
        4           for(i=0;i<*n;i++) {
        (dbx) print *n
        *n = 3
        (dbx) where   
        =>[1] mycode(x = 0xb2d3e0, n = 0xb2dc68), line 4 in "a.c"
        [2] S_interface(0xaa0370, 0xd2f0f0, 0x2, 0xc3b740, 0x2, 0x0), at
0x125504
        [3] quick_call(0xaa0370, 0xd2b098, 0x124c3c, 0x1, 0xefffe6f0, 0x0),
at 0x614e8
        [4] Eval(0xaa0370, 0xaa0370, 0xaa0370, 0xa, 0xd2af64, 0xc31040), at
0x675a4
        [5] evalArgClasses(0x1, 0x117, 0x2, 0xb44bd0, 0x0, 0xd2af64), at
0x6a564
        [6] findMethod(0xefffeae0, 0x1, 0xefffead4, 0xaa0370, 0xc1c748,

messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

I am trying to use xyplot in the second way summarized by Mr. Kshatriya 
(attached below) and ended up with something I didn't expect.

I have a dateset with 4 groups and for each group I hope to superpose 5 more 
lines with different symbols (for example, lty=1 to 6). I pool all the 
y-values for the lines into a long variable, and add one more variale 
(factor) "type" to identify the type of lines. Everything was fine except 
that I got dotted lines for the frames of the plots, which made the plots 
very messy. I attached below the commands I used. Could  someone please tell 
me how I can get the solid lines for the plot frames?

===============

xyplot(y~x|group, data=summF.dat, subscripts=T, groups=summF.dat$type, 
style=1,strip.names=c(F, F),

panel=function(x, y, subscripts, groups,...){

true_ groups[subscripts]=="true"

q1<-groups[subscripts]=="Q1"

q2<-groups[subscripts]=="Q2"

q3<-groups[subscripts]=="Q3"

q4<-groups[subscripts]=="Q4"

q5<-groups[subscripts]=="Q5"

panel.xyplot(x[true], y[true], type="l", lty=1)

panel.superpose(x[q1], y[q1], subscripts[q1], groups, type="l",   lty=2)

panel.superpose(x[q2], y[q2], subscripts[q2], groups, type="l", lty=3)

 panel.superpose(x[q3], y[q3], subscripts[q3], groups, type="l", lty=4)

panel.superpose(x[q4], y[q4], subscripts[q4], groups, type="l", lty=5)

panel.superpose(x[q5], y[q5], subscripts[q5], groups, type="l", lty=6) }

)

Great thanks in advance!

Chunlei Ke

> From: M Kshatriya <mkshatriya at zoology.up.ac.za>
> To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
> Subject: Re: [S] xyplot command - summary
> Date: Tue, 22 Feb 2000 09:25:13 +0200
>
> I would like to thank Lutz Prechelt and  Bill Venables for their  response
> to my question
> about plotting (x,y) locations and  a boundary using the  xyplot command.
> There appears to be two ways of doing this:
>
> 1) Perhaps the simplest one would be
>
>
>
> xyplot(xboundary ~ yboundary, xlab = "x", ylab = "y",
>       panel = function(x, y, ...) {
>             panel.xyplot(x, y, ..., type = "l")
>             panel.xyplot(xlocations, ylocations, pch=1, col=2, ...)
>       })
> - Prechelt and  Bill Venables
>
> This assumes that your x's and y's are free-standing vectors on
> the search path.
>
> 2)  A second  solution is to put xlocations and xboundary together in the
> same data frame,
> and similarly for y, and have a factor, say `type' that distinguishes them.
> You could then do
>
> xyplot(x ~ y, dat, panel = function(x, y, ...) {
>  panel.xyplot(x[dat$type == "b"], y[dat$type == "b"], ..., type = "l")
>  panel.xyplot(x[dat$type == "l"], y[dat$type == "l"], ..., pch=1, col=2)
> })
>
> That looks much more complicated than the first way, but it pays
> off if you want to do a conditioning plot and you need to pass
> subscripts down to the panel function.
> - Bill Venables.
>
> Many thanks to both.
>

messages.subject: Re: [S] Handling of missing values in table()
messages.subject_clean: [S] Handling of missing values in table()
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Brian Ripley, Judi Scheffer, Mike Hoekstra (who reported an
exchange with S-PLUS Tech support), Anne York, Don McQueen and Bill
Dunlap for their replies.  It may be helpful to others who are
seeking light on this problem to have a progress report on what is
a serious bug is S-PLUS 2000.

Bill Dunlap suggested:

>?  If the is.na() result has T in positions 6 and 7 then
>       test$V1[is.na(test$V1)] <- NA
>should fix things up.  I think the data import code may have used
>the wrong bit pattern for NA's and some of the Splus accepts the
>bad pattern as NA and some doesn't.

The bad bit pattern explanation is the only one that seems to fit.
Below are further details.

Brian Ripley commented:

>NA vs NaN?  S-PLUS prints them the same but handles them 
>differently. Importing tends to give NaNs not NAs.
>So just printing the vector does not tell you what is inside it.
and that
>Dump turns NaNs into NAs.

He, and Bill Dunlap, suggested that I test 
>is.nan(test1$V1)
[1] F F F F F F F

So that rules out the NaN explanation, at least for my data.

As Don McQueen pointed out, V2 in test1 had the AsIs class.  This
seems not relevant, but we'll wait and see!

Mike Hoekstra reported an exchange with MathSoft engineers.

Dumping the data set (use dump() and source() or dump.data()
and data.restore()) is one way to fix the problem, as my message
already demonstrated.

Be warned!! Apparently this bug is not in S-PLUS 4.5 r2.

I consider that the printed output from table() should always report
on observations that are not accounted for in the table.  This would
be in general a useful warning that we have here a function which
(unlike mean(), etc.) ignores missing values if left to its own
devices.  It would have warned that something was wrong in the
present instance.

Here is the substance of my message
> I am using S-PLUS2000 (Release 2) under Windows 98.
> 
> # Create test1 by reading in an Excel file
> # NB: Sourcing the data structure below
> # gives a test1 that behaves in the same way as xy
> # See below for the dump of test1

> > table(test1$V1,exclude=NULL)
>  1 2 3 4 5 NA 
>  1 1 1 1 1  0
> 
> > is.factor(test$V1)  # Just checking
> [1] F

messages.subject_clean: [S] Introducing S+SeqTrial - Analyze, Visualize And Monitor Clinical Trials
messages.body_plain:
MathSoft is pleased to announce to s-news a brand new module for S-PLUS:
S+SeqTrial.

S+SeqTrial
----------

Now, you can bring beneficial treatments to market sooner with MathSoft's
new S+SeqTrial software.

"S+SeqTrial is the perfect tool for designing and monitoring clinical trials
including a comprehensive selection of validated designs integrated with
powerful data analysis capabilities," says Gracie Liebermann, Genentech.
"Its easy-to-use graphical user interface and professional graphics are
ideal for communicating results to non-statisticians and FDA reporting.
S+SeqTrial will help our company to make decisions to terminate or continue
trials sooner, potentially saving lives and reducing clinical trial costs."

For more information or to order a free white paper, please contact us at
1-800-569-0123, e-mail smarston at splus.mathsoft.com, or visit our web site at
www.splus.mathsoft.com/products/seqtrial.  For a limited time only, if you
order a copy of S+SeqTrial you'll receive up to 40% off our commercial
price.  Hurry, offer ends April 30, 2000.

We'll be demonstrating the new technology at the DIA Show on March 12-14th
(Hilton Head, SC), March 15th (RTP, NC), March 16th (Princeton, NJ) and
March 28th (Atlanta, GA).  Details available at
http://www.splus.mathsoft.com/events or call 1-800-569-0123.

Why S+SeqTrial?

A Complete Software Environment

S+SeqTrial offers a complete computing environment for applying group
sequential methods, including a fully object-oriented language with
specialized objects (such as design objects and boundary objects) and
methods (such as operating characteristics and power curve plots).
S+SeqTrial has a graphical user interface that facilitates selection,
evaluation, and comparison of group sequential designs.

Selection of Group Sequential Designs

S+SeqTrial supports clinical trial design for single arm, two arm,
regression analyses, and the probability models that can be used include the
normal, lognormal, binomial, Poisson, and proportional hazards models.
S+SeqTrial offers the complete set of sequential designs based on the
unified family of Kittelson and Emerson (1999), which includes as special
cases the O'Brien and Fleming (1979), triangular (Whitehead and Stratton,
1983), and other commonly used group sequential designs.  Designs can also
be specified using a family of error spending functions.

Evaluation of Candidate Designs

Every clinical trial presents unique issues with respect to patient safety
and design efficiency.  S+SeqTrial is designed to facilitate the clinical
trialist's selection of the best stopping rule for any given setting.

Monitoring a Clinical Trial

S+SeqTrial allows the flexible implementation of stopping rules using a
constrained boundary approach that includes the error spending functions of
Lan and DeMets (1983) and Pampallona, Tsiatis, and Kim (1995) as a special
case. Because S+SeqTrial is fully integrated with the analytic capabilities
of the S-PLUS language, the user is able to analyze the data and apply the
stopping rule in a single command.

Reporting Results

S+SeqTrial provides a comprehensive selection of methods for the computation
of exact P values, exact confidence intervals, and estimators of treatment
effect which adjust for the biases introduced by interim analyses.

Accuracy and Reliability

The accuracy of the recursive numerical integration routines used by
S+SeqTrial have been validated against standard group sequential designs and
estimation techniques previously reported in the statistical literature.

messages.subject: [S] Analysis of Deviance on GLM object
messages.subject_clean: [S] Analysis of Deviance on GLM object
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to set up an analysis of deviance example using S for a  
class.  I have a set of bird counts at 4 sites, 4 days and 4 time periods 
during the day.  I get the following ANODEV table using anova() on the glm 
result from my sample data:

--------------------------------------------------------
> anova(glm.out, test="F")
Analysis of Deviance Table

Poisson model

Response: obs

Terms added sequentially (first to last)
     Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev  F Value     Pr(F) 
NULL                    15   130.8296                   
site  3 70.19873        12    60.6308 11.43079 0.0068071
 day  3 27.33229         9    33.2986  4.45065 0.0570735
time  3 16.91165         6    16.3869  2.75381 0.1345394
--------------------------------------------------------

Now, this isn't really pretty, so I wrote up a function to put
everything into a more desired format, recalculating the F-values
along the way.  Here's what I get:

--------------------------------------------------------
> anodev(glm.out)
           d.f. Deviance Deviance/df     F-test  Pr(F) 
Total_corr   15 130.8296                              
      site    3  70.1987     23.3996     8.5677 0.0137
       day    3  27.3323      9.1108     3.3359 0.0975
      time    3  16.9117      5.6372     2.0640 0.2065
  Residual    6  16.3869      2.7312                  
--------------------------------------------------------

Note the difference in F-values.  Usually, when I've done
F-tests by hand vs. the anova() function, it's off by a few decimals,
which can be explained by rounding error.  

A search of the S-news archives turned up an e-mail from Petr Smilauer 
concerning a similar problem back in 1995.  Trevor Hastie indicated that 
this was a bug in deviance.glmlist, where the F-value was adjusted by the 
over- or underdispersion estimated.  Since this was not corrected in any of 
the versions of S since then (I've got both 5.1 on Unix and Splus 2000 in 
Windows, and got the same answer), is this dispersion adjustment really a 
bug, or an example of inappropriate analysis?  Using a Chi-square test 
results in a completely different answer:

--------------------------------------------------------
> anova.glm(glm.out, test="Chisq")
Analysis of Deviance Table

Poisson model

Response: obs

Terms added sequentially (first to last)
     Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev      Pr(Chi) 
NULL                    15   130.8296             
site  3 70.19873        12    60.6308 0.0000000000
 day  3 27.33229         9    33.2986 0.0000050147
time  3 16.91165         6    16.3869 0.0007369345
--------------------------------------------------------

Any comments on what the appropriate analysis would be here would be 
greatly appreciated.

                                                        Rich            

            Columbia Basin Research, Puget Sound Plaza, suite 1820
            Seattle, Washington  98101               (206)616-7492
                    http://www.cbr.washington.edu/~townsend 
              --------------------------------------------------
            Alcohol and calculus don't mix. Never drink and derive.

messages.body_plain:
A few months ago I went to a talk about electronic NDA submissions where PDF
documents were used with hyperlinks to link discussions of statistical
results in the text of the report to tables and figures in the appendices.

I'd like to use this idea for smaller statistical reports using Microsoft
Word on a NT/9x/2000 platform.  I would not only like to link text to tables
and figures, but also to Splus/SAS data sets and code.  I would also like to
add the ability to not only view the code in a text format, but also to be
able to submit the code in BATCH from within the document (assuming the
reviewer has PC Splus available) and have the output screen automatically
diplayed to the screen.  This would greatly facilitate internal/external
reviews of the statistical analysis by putting the details at the fingertips
of the reviewing statisticians.

I'm sure that this has been done before, but can anybody give me some hints
on completing this task.  I plan to use Visual Basic to help link Word to
the external applications, but I'll be teaching myself VB on the fly.

Any hints would be greatly appreciated, I'll summarize and make a Word
template available when I complete this task.

Thanks in advance,

Matt Austin

messages.subject: Re: [S] Dynamic Statistical Report
messages.body_plain:
Matt,

As MS Word lacks a true batch mode I think you will find that it will take a lot
more work to do what you want in Word compared with using LaTeX.  The features 
of LaTeX that are relevant to your needs are:

- the \input{filename} command for assembling tables created by S-Plus or SAS,
  or for including definitions of variable values to be included in results; I 
produce
  most of my tables using the display library by Richard Heiberger and myself,
  and my Hmisc library, which produce LaTeX code ready for \input'ing.
  My Design library produces LaTeX code specifying many types of fitted
  regression models  in algebraic form.  LaTeX can also handle verbatim
  insertion of files with no re-formatting (for plain tabular listings).
- the \includegraphics{filename} comand to include postscript or other graphics;
  whenever any of the graphics or tables are updated, running the latex system
  command will update an entire report, recompute cross-references and
  table of contents, etc.
- the hyperref style in LaTeX makes all bibliographic citations, references,
   sections, subsections, tables of contents, indexes, etc., automatically 
hyperlinked
   with no work by the user
- hyperlinks created by hyperref (plus any manually entered ones such as URLs)
   automatically become bookmarks when the pdf file is produced
- you can have "if-then" constructs in LaTeX for conditional output generation
- the output just looks better

A report called Statistical Tables and Plots using S-Plus and LaTeX 
demonstrates much of this and includes the uncompiled listing of itself, i.e., 
all the LaTeX code used to produce the report.  If you navigate this pdf 
document you'll see that all the figures in the table of figures are 
hyperlinked as are sections.   For an example with more
hyperlinks including a hyperlinked detailed topic index at the back of the 
document, see
the documents by Alzola & Harrell in http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s. 
 There are two versions of this document - one for printing and one for 
on-screen viewing.  For the latter, I used the LaTeX pdfscreen style which uses 
bigger fonts for easy screen viewing, and invokes hyperref.  It is extremely 
easy to run the pdflatex command on a slightly modified master file (where 
styles are requested) to produce an on-screen report from the same material 
used to generate a printed report.

Regarding segmented out code and submission of code from with a report 
document, this is "literate programming".  See 
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/LiveDoc.html for a web page 
containing links to information and software regarding literate programming as 
well as to the report on statistical reporting.  I have not used literate 
programming myself but hope to soon.
The Alzola & Harrell document shows how to do conditional batch processing of
sections of S-Plus code, with each section managing its own listing and 
graphics files.

I tried using MS Word for about 2 years before realizing how incredibly 
inefficient it is. LaTeX is free and there is an amazing amount of helpful 
macros etc. available on the Internet, not to mention a very helpful news group 
comp.text.tex.  LaTeX will handle reports from a few pages to many hundred 
pages, as it is a tool of choice for writing books.  For Win95/98/NT I use 
FPTeX (see the above web page), thanks to
Brian Ripley who pointed me in that direction.

Frank E Harrell Jr
Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Department of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.subject: [S] summary: trellis plot using splom
messages.body_plain:
Hello, 

Many many thanks to 
Andy Liaw,
Brian Ripley,
Marcel Baumgartner,  
Renaud Lancelot
for their nice answers for my questions about splom plotting. This
community is realy great!

1.Andy's answer:
I got it to work on a bogus dataset.  Hopefully this will help:

x<-as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(100),25,4))
y<-as.factor(rep(LETTERS[1:5],5))
splom(~x,groups=y,
        panel=function(x,y,subscripts,...){
        panel.superpose(x,y,subscripts,...)
        panel.loess(x,y)
        }
)
2. Brian's answer:

You should have some ...'s in there.  From Venables & Ripley:

splom(~ swiss.df, aspect="fill",
   panel = function(x, y, ...) {
      panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)
      panel.loess(x, y, ...)
   }
)

and you should have panel= only once (and not panel.superpose).
3. Marcel's answer:
for the first question: you use twice the argument panel=... . This
certainly causes
the problem. You might need something like:

 ..., groups = Mon,
      panel=function(x,y,...) {panel.superpose(x,y,...)
                                       panel.loess(x,y)} ...

Note however that the loess curves will be done for all points, and not
separately
according to the group argument.

For the 2nd questions: there is no easy way around. But you change the
line

text(0.5/p + d, 0.5/p + d, varnames[i])

in the function panel.pairs() into

text(0.5/p + d, 0.5/p + d, varnames[i],cex=0.6)

and this decreases the size of the varnames.

4.Renauld's answer:
1. I suspect a problem with the argument panel = panel.superpose. Since
panel.superpose is a function and that you don't provide any argument to
the call, it probably takes the second panel call as its argument (well
I guess I am not clear !). I suggest that you should remove this line
(panel = panel.superpose).

I had problems with splom: when I added lines to the scatterplot, most
of them crossed the whole plotting area. After a suggestion from Marcel
Baumgartner, I solved it this way (in the following code, Coef is a
matrix):

splom(~ Coef, 
  panel = function(x, y){
    panel.xyplot(x, y, col=16, cex=1/2)
    lm.loc <- lm(y ~ x)
    x.seq <- seq(min(x), max(x), length=100)
    pred <- predict(lm.loc, data.frame(x = x.seq))
    ok <- rep(T, length(pred))
    ok[pred < min(y)] <- F
    ok[pred > max(y)] <- F
    lines(x.seq[ok], pred[ok], lwd=2)
    }
)

You will easily adapt it for loess instead of lm.

My question:
> trellis.device(postscript, width=5, height=5, hor=F, file="pair.ps")
> attach(resFW)
> month<-as.factor(resFW$Mon)
> n<-length(levels(month))
> scat<-resFW[,3:5]
> pair<-splom(~scat, varnames=list("lab\n(%)", "blender\n(%)",
> "separator\n(%)"),
>            groups=Mon,
>            panel=panel.superpose,
>            panel=function(x,y) {
>               panel.splom(x,y, cex=0.5)
>               panel.loess(x,y, span=1)},
>            key=list(points=Rows(trellis.par.get("superpose.symbol"),
1:n),
>           text=list(c("August", "May"), c(1,2)),columns=n))
> print(pair)
> dev.off()
> 
> My questions:
> 1. Whenever I run the program, I was told:
>  > source("pair.s")
>  Error in subpanel(x[, j] + offsets[j], x[, i] + of..: Can't pass data
of
>  mode
>         "function" to old-S function
>  Dumped
> I can not figure out why that happened. When I take the
> panel=function(x,y){...} off, then everything is fine, but I do want to
> give a loess in the subpanel, and I also want to change the size of the
> symbol in the panel. Can anybody give me some hints? 
> > 
> 2. I want to change the size of the variable names (the character size)
in
> the plot, how can I do that?
>

On Mon, 6 Mar 2000 aczarn at cs.uwa.edu.au wrote:

> i am using Splus version 5.0 on a linux box

> but i have decided that i need to allow for
> random effects in my model
> 
> i have discovered that for aov Splus has another
> in-built function i can use called raov which allows for
> random effects
> 
> however, is there a similar function in-built in
> Splus for manova, that allows for manova analysis
> with random effects ???

You can also use aov for random effects, and that does (as far as I recall)
allow multiple responses.  You need to add an Error term.

Precisely what MANOVA means is a matter of definition, but as for S-PLUS
it means 

DETAILS:
       A manova object is essentially the same as an  aov  object
       from  a  multiresponse model, only the class is different.
       The most important difference is that there  is  a  method
       for summary specific to manova objects.

you can also use manova with Error terms.

(I think the M means `multivariate', but the actual analysis given is
`multiple' apart from the multivariate tests in summary.anova.)

Brian Ripley.  

It is as simple as checking the "Create Editable Graphics" option which it
seems can be done in a number of ways...I have included some responses below.

options header and Graph/Options.  Check the "Create Editable Graphics" and
you will be able to create graphics using code and edit them gui afterwards.
This is somewhat of a double edged sword, I was getting undesirable effects
with this option turned on (multiple axis lines showing up while creating
multiple axis labels) but see if it works for you.

enable you to do exactly as you wish. The Option is on the first page
(Options) and in the box Traditional Graphics it is titled Create Editable
Graphics. When I enabled this In S-Plus 2000 release 1 it enabled me to
change the colour of points, axis labels etc. Also it is possible to create
the plots which are on the toolbars by using the GuiPlot functions - but
this probably isn't what you requested. You can find out a bit more by
searching the S-Plus Help for 'Editable Graphics' from the toolbar. 

Either start with an editable graphics when you launch the graphsheet,
or convert them later.  It is in the manuals.

messages.subject: [S] Splus5.1 vs 3.4
messages.body_plain:
In my original post I asked what positive features/enhancements of
Splus5.1 had people found.  Overall, the responses reinforced the
notion that we'll release 5.1 but the default will be 3.4.

The positives noted were -

- compiling/loading externals is easier
- It's available for Linux.
- The latest rpart is only released for 5.1.
- The functions bootstrap, multicomp, censorReg, importData, lmRobMM 
- multiple comparisons after anova
- more survival analysis capabilities 
- We can import large objects using 5.1, and manipulate them,
  that are impossible on 3.4.  Once the null-string-attributes
  glitch is known to users, the speed is superior for large objects.
- 5.1 has a pdf graphics driver that is very handy.

Thanks to everyone who replied:Patrick Connolly, Nicole DePriest,
Peter Perkins,  Brian D Ripley, B.Rowlingson, Todd Taylor,
Steve Wofsy.

- Beth Atkinson

******************************************************************************

* Personally, I'd stick with 3.4 until they get some of the kinks worked out
  of 5.1.

* this is v5.1 on Irix6.x:

  my experience so far has not been so positive.  it seems to use more
  memory (despite what the documentation claims), the help system stinks,
  and there were a number of teethng problems (that StatSci -- as usual --
  denied were problems at all) with the actual installation.  and if it
  creates one more MySwork directory (when i've asked it politely not to),
  i'm going to go beserk.

  haven't found anything from the "what's new" stuff that has really
  improved my life.  but it's still S and it still works.  oh, compiling
  and loading externals is much easier.

* The main ways 5.1 has affected me:

  1) It's slower for most things I do, especially Trellis graphics.
  2) It's more memory intensive for most things I do.
  3) It's available for Linux.

  The ever-advancing state of hardware has made (1) and (2) minor
  considerations.

  Number (3) is the main benefit to me (and it's a big one).

  I've not yet availed myself of the new S4 features, but the
  improved OOP model is probably a good thing.  I know the old one
  was certainly difficult to work with.

  Migrating old functions and data has not been too hard.
  
* I'd be very interested in what you find.  We haven't changed from 3.4
  either, not being too keen on the debacle over the new class which
  could have been done a whole lot better.  We have numerous functions
  accrued over years, and it's quite useful knowing just how old they
  are.  If they have to be redone, we lose the date information and with
  it any feeling of what our competence was at the time it was written.
  As yet, I've not noticed any compelling reason to change, but you
  might find one.
  
* The latest rpart is only released for 5.1?
  bootstrap, multicomp, censorReg (but maybe not if you want to keep the
  boss happy), importData, lmRobMM, are ones I have used.
  
* It's very hard to find stuff thats better in 5.1 than 3.4. Some of my
  users report processes hogging even more memory in 5.1 than 3.4 - this
  can be alleviated by rewriting loop code though, but its work. The help
  system (now a java applet) has some major problems - first of course,
  you need java enabled on your web browser (which currently crashes my
  netscape installation 9 times out of 10, but thats probably my
  fault..), then there's a few other minor complications if you are
  running Splus on a different box to netscape.  Netscape wont
  necessarily find the help files, because Splus might not even be
  installed on the machine running Netscape.

  Splus 5.1 incorporates the latest revision of the S language, version
  4. This causes plenty of headaches. Library code that used the object
  oriented features of the previous version needs serious amounts of
  rewriting. One of our locally developed libraries 'Oswald', was written
  according to the old O-O system, and conforms to all the methods and
  dogma laid down by that system. Yet porting it to Splus 5.1 hasnt
  happened yet, since the automatic conversion tools that Splus 5.1 has
  dont work on it, and hand crafting a conversion is a big task.  I've
  also been developing O-O code for a different application from scratch,
  and that too is a nightmare. I dont think many people are doing this -
  since a message I posted on S-news about it a couple of weeks ago drew
  no response.  All I wanted to do was to make a class that inherited
  from 'data.frame', but this seems impossible.

  Miscellaneous bugs in 3.4 have carried over to 5.1 - the irregular
  image plot in postscript is still there (and this was reported in 1996
  by someone), and there are lots of problems with the Linux port. The
  Linux port was the only reason we switched - since they dont do 3.4 for
  Linux. I've recently reported a bug with signal handling in Splus 5.1
  for linux. If you interrupt (with Ctrl-C) an Splus function that does
  something like unix("sleep 10") (or equivalently, sleep(10)), then
  Splus may crash - if not at that point but at the next generated
  error!  I've also had random system terminations due to address errors
  that I couldn't track down.

  Some of our lecturers are still having to use 3.4 because of library
  code they havent converted to 5.1. This caused much embarrassment when
  I taught all the students how to use 5.1 and then they have to be told
  to use 3.4, with all the hassle of switching between .Data for
  different versions...

  Oh, I could go on....

* multiple comparisons after anova

  more survival analysis capabilities

  The censorReg() function if any of your users need to fit models to 
  censored data (this is common in the environmental field, when 
  analytical labs report "non-detections", i.e., the best they can do 
  is provide an upper bound; I don't know if it happens with medical 
  labs)
  
* We can import large objects using 5.1, and manipulate them,
  that are impossible on 3.4.  Once the null-string-attributes
  glitch is known to users, the speed is superior for large objects.

  5.1 has a pdf graphics driver that is very handy.

  The major negative is the unrliable export back to 3.4-type objects.

messages.subject: [S] Cox & Wermuth short course announcement
messages.body_plain:
OTTAWA SHORT COURSE ON APPLYING STATISTICS 2000

Monday & Tuesday, May 15&16 2000
9am to 5pm
Ottawa, Ontario
Canada

Sponsored by 
Department of Epidemiology and Community Health of the University of Ottawa
and the Loeb Health Research Institute at The Ottawa Hospital

MULTIVARIATE DEPENDENCIES

Lecturers: David Cox, Nuffield College, Oxford and Nanny Wermuth, ZUMA -
Center for Survey Research, Mannheim

Registration Fee: $300.00 (Cdn) - The fee to Graduate Students is $150.00.
Includes the lecturer's book 
"Multivariate Dependencies - Models, Analysis and Interpretation", Chapman
and Hall, 1996

The aim of the course:

The course will provide a systematic discussion of a basis for the analysis
and interpretation of complex multivariate data. The course is designed for
those making extensive use of statistical methods in health and social
science research who need to meaningfully interact with both other
statisticians and scientists / decision makers. Common issues and themes
that arise in almost any form of careful data analysis, complex or
otherwise, will be discussed. 

The course is intended for those concerned with the analysis and
interpretation of complex data, especially but not entirely observational
data. The applications from the social and health sciences are wide-ranging
including, for example, studies of medical interventions and of sociological
or psychological development. While the primary emphasis will be on
statistical methods for direct use in applications, some issues of
theoretical interest will also be addressed. One central theme will be the
role of independence graphs and on processes by which the data could have
been generated. This theme suggests the recasting and restructuring of
fairly standard and well known statistical techniques to better focus and
report on important data analysis issues. 

No software presentations will be given, the emphasis being largely on
methods which can be implemented within standard packages. A fairly similar
course was given last Fall at the Fields Institute in Toronto
(http://www.fields.utoronto.ca/cis-scourse.html#MARKOV). 

While the course is based in part on the lecturers' book "Multivariate
Dependencies - Models, Analysis and Interpretation" (Chapman and Hall,
1996), a number of important developments since the book will be described.
As well as core material a number of specific research questions will be
discussed in detail; the corresponding data can be obtained via the internet
(soon at http://www.lri.ca/).

For further information and registration email the course organizer, Keith
O'Rourke at multdep at lri.ca.

messages.body_plain:
Weidong,

When SAS changed to version 7 it added the restriction that SAS code
must be in files named *.sas.  sas.get used a temporary file named *.tmp.
I updated sas.get the other day to fix that problem.  Assuming that's what
caused your problem, please download sas.get again from our web
page for now (http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/Hmisc.html ;
for some reason StatLib is not obtaining updated
versions of the Hmisc library since Dec. 1999) and try again.

One thing is confusing about your SAS program.  You created an
ASCII file using a PUT statement.  sas.get goes directly from your
SAS dataset, so your PUT statement did not benefit sas.get.

-Frank

messages.subject: [S] Statistical Data Mining Course by Prof. Brian Ripley, Oxford, UK 27-28/03/2000
messages.subject_clean: [S] Statistical Data Mining Course by Prof. Brian Ripley, Oxford, UK 27-28/03/2000
messages.body_plain:
MathSoft is pleased to announce:

Statistical Data Mining

Presented by Professor Brian D Ripley

Oxford, 27-28 March 2000

Further Details and on-line registration:

http://www.mathsoft.co.uk/splus/main/courses.htm

Data mining, also known as `knowledge discovery in databases' is one of many
terms for finding structure in large-scale datasets on the boundaries of
statistics, engineering, machine learning and computer science. This course
will concentrate on methods for finding the structure (as distinct from
manipulating the databases) using the tools which are available in or for
S-PLUS 2000 and 5.1.

The assumed background knowledge is at the level of linear regression and
the ability to run scripts in S-PLUS 2000.

The course will consist of lectures and hands-on experience with desktop PCs
throughout the course. Course notes will be provided as well as the S-PLUS
libraries and scripts used in the course.

Synopsis:

Overview of Data Mining

What is data mining?
Supervised and unsupervised problems.
How can visualization help?
Looking for needles in haystacks.
Clusters?

Neural Networks

What is a neural network?
Families of neural networks.
The most common: feed-forward neural networks.
Overview of other types of neural networks

Feed-forward neural networks in S-PLUS

The `nnet' library for S-PLUS.
Regression examples.
Importance of weight decay.
Using nnet for classification problems.
Choosing the degree of flexibility.

Classification trees 

Idea of recursive partitioning algorithms.
Choosing the splits.
How large a tree should we grow?
Pruning algorithms.
How hard should a tree be pruned?
Implementations of classification trees in S-PLUS

k-nearest neighbour methods

Background theory for k-NN methods
Implementation details, such as handling ties.
The `class' library for S-PLUS.
Using 3NN methods to estimate the Bayes risk.
Choosing prototypes for nearest-neighbour methods
Learning vector quantization.

Assessing performance of data-mining tools

Design of methodological studies.
Training, testing and validation.
Cross-validation.
Estimating the Bayes risk and achieved performance.
Is the improvement significant?
Case studies.

Professor Brian D. Ripley

Professor Brian Ripley holds the Chair of Applied Statistics at the
University of Oxford, and is well known for his books which include `Pattern
Recognition and Neural Networks' (CUP, 1996) and `Modern Applied Statistics
with S-PLUS' (Springer, 1994, 1997, 1999) and `S Programming' (Springer,
2000) with Bill Venables . He is the author of the tree-pruning software
currently in S-PLUS and the `nnet' and `class' libraries supplied with
S-PLUS 2000. 

 
Yours,

In regards to the question of whether S-Plus could do trilinear or piper
plots, it appears (based on responses to this question in s-news)
that the answer is s-plus functions have been developed to do a trilinear
plot but not a piper plot. Thanks for all of your help.

In s-news,  3 people (Bob Garrett, Julie Greene,and Sama Low Choy) provided
functions for trilinear plots. These
functions are listed below:

Ginny

PS. FYI, there are programs in other languages to do piper plots USGS also
has a FORTRAN computer program for piper plots.  And, Bob
Garrett provided the following information about 2 other programs.

                                                                                
                              
                    "Garrett,                                                   
                              
                    Robert"              To:     "'vlmcguir at usgs.gov'" 
<vlmcguir at usgs.gov>                    
                    <garrett@NRCa        cc:

                    03/01/00

Ginny:

I took a look in GeoRef, as I thought I remembered something in Computers &
Geosciences, and only found one post-1993 entry on piper+computer that
mentioned code.  The citation is below, and I just took a quick look (I
have
them here as an old IAMG member) and the algorithms to go from ternary
plots
to the diamond are there, pp. 995-997.

    MHPT.BAS; a computer program for modified Hill-Piper diagram for
classification of ground

Also, I have a colleague here who wrote a Visual Basic program to do Piper

1. ========================================================================

Virginia:

I read your post with interest, and the explanation that you forwarded
later.  I was once asked by a colleague here at the GSC if I could plot
Piper diagrams with S-Plus, and I have to admit I said no.  What I do have
is a couple of ternary diagram functions that I have used extensively over
the years and have shared with many.  I never took the Piper step, as
soils,
sediments and rocks are my usual stock in geochemical trade.

Anyway, I will watch with interest to see if someone has coded a Piper

S-Plus
can plot them (there are just a handful of S-Plus users in the Survey).  If

================================================================================
Dear Ginny McGuire,

Thank you for your multiple follow-up questions regarding how to modify
the format of 'ternary.plot' to more closely resemble a Piper graph.
While programming specific functions is outside the realm of technical
support, I have given some suggestions in the attached script file
"piper.plot.ssc".

You can run the following example calling the function
'piper.plot' contained in the script file as follows, after sourcing in
the attached script file "piper.plot.ssc":

#Create data set so that columns are cation composition
# start with dataset :
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

demo <- data.sheet(Ca=c(.8, .5, .675), Mg=c(.26, .5, .4725),
           Na.K=c(.89, 1, .2025))

# Create Compositions

           demo$Ca.comp <- unlist(apply(demo, 1, function(data)
                                          round((data[1]/sum(data[1:3]))
*100,
                                          digits=0)))
           demo$Mg.comp <- unlist(apply(demo, 1, function(data)
                                          round((data[2]/sum(data[1:3]))
*100,
                                          digits=0)))
           demo$Na.K.comp <- unlist(apply(demo, 1, function(data)
                                          round((data[3]/sum(data[1:3]))
*100,
                                          digits=0)))
# Create Group column to vary symbols by in the piper plot

           demo$Group <- c("A", "B", "C")

# Call 'piper.plot' function:

           piper.plot(demo, xColumn="Ca.comp", yColumn="Mg.comp",
                               zColumn="Na.K.comp", GroupColumn="Group")

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

An additional copy of the 'piper.plot' function is pasted below.

To be honest, I am not very familiar with the format of a Piper Graph, so
these modifications are only meant to give you ideas. As you mentioned, I
would suggest that you try contacting s-news to see if someone has already
programmed a more convenient form of 'ternary.plot' for you.

I hope this information helps! Please feel free to contact us again should
you have further questions.

Kind Regards,

Julie Greene

********************************************************************
  Julie Greene                           email: support at statsci.com
  Technical Support Engineer               FAX: (206) 283-8691
  MathSoft, Inc.                        phones: (206) 283-8802
  Data Analysis Products Division               1-800-569-0123
********************************************************************

piper.plot <- function(DataSet, xColumn="x", yColumn="y", zColumn="z",
           GraphSheet = "", grid.num=9, title.offset = 0.15,
           label.offset=0.032, digits=2, axis.range=100, GroupColumn=NULL){

           # Rough sketch of function to create Piper plot.

           if (is.character(DataSet))
                     DataSet <- get(DataSet)

           x <- DataSet[,xColumn]
           y <- DataSet[,yColumn]
           z <- DataSet[,zColumn]
           w <- DataSet[,GroupColumn]

           grid.num <- grid.num + 1

           if (!all(length(x)==c(length(y),length(z)))){
                               stop("The x, y, and z columns specified are
of
different lengths.")
           }

           if (length(x) + length(z) + length(z) < 3){
                     stop("One or more of the columns has no data.")
           }

           row.sums <- x+y+z

           if (!all(row.sums==row.sums[1])){
                     stop("The row sums are not all equal.  All rows must
sum
to the same value.")
           }

           axis.range <- axis.range
           # Calculate 2D XY data from 3D triangular data

           graph.y <- x * 0.86602
           graph.x <- z + (graph.y * tan(0.52360))

           axis.center <- axis.range * 0.5
           axis.x.top <- axis.range * 0.5 * 1.73205

           # Triples is defined but not used.  It could be used to label
points.

           triples <- paste("(",x,", ",y,           ", ",z,")",sep="")

           # Set data for axes, grids and ticks

           axis.x <- c(0, axis.range, axis.range * 0.5, 0)
           axis.y <- c(0, 0, axis.range * 0.86602, 0)

           # Labels and titles

           x.title.x <- (axis.range - axis.range*.75) -
title.offset*axis.range
           x.title.y <- axis.range * 0.25 * 1.732050
           x.title.z <- xColumn

           y.title.x <- axis.range * .75 + title.offset*axis.range
           y.title.y <- axis.range * 0.25 * 1.732050
           y.title.z <- yColumn

           z.title.x <- axis.range * 0.5
           z.title.y <- 0 - axis.range*title.offset
           z.title.z <- zColumn

           ## Grids

           # Z axis grid positions

           grid.seq <- (1:grid.num)/grid.num

           z.axis.x <- axis.range * grid.seq
           z.axis.y <- rep(0, grid.num)

           # X and Y axis grid positions

           x.axis.y <- (axis.range * 0.5 * 1.73205) * grid.seq
           y.axis.y <- x.axis.y

           y.axis.x <- (axis.range * 0.5) * grid.seq

           ## The calculation below may need revision.  Check this!!!
           x.axis.x <- axis.range - y.axis.x

           grid.x <- c(rbind(x.axis.x,y.axis.x, NA), rbind(z.axis.x,
y.axis.x, NA),
                     rbind(z.axis.x, c(rev(x.axis.x)[-1], NA), NA))

           # Drop extra NA
           #grid.x <- grid.x[-length(grid.x)]

           grid.y <- c(rbind(x.axis.y, y.axis.y, NA), rbind(z.axis.y,
y.axis.y, NA),
                     rbind(z.axis.y, c(rev(x.axis.y)[-1],NA), NA))

           # Drop extra NA
           #grid.y <- grid.y[-length(grid.y)]

           # Axis labels

           # Remove last row to prevent axis titles from overlapping

           col.length <- length(x.axis.x)
           x.axis.x <- x.axis.x[-col.length]
           x.axis.y <- x.axis.y[-col.length]
           y.axis.x <- y.axis.x[-col.length]
           y.axis.y <- y.axis.y[-col.length]
           z.axis.x <- z.axis.x[-col.length]
           z.axis.y <- z.axis.y[-col.length]

           x.label <- y.label <- z.label <- round(axis.range*grid.seq,
digits)

           y.label <- rev(y.label)
           y.label <- y.label[-1]

           x.axis.x <- x.axis.x + axis.range * label.offset
           y.axis.x <- y.axis.x - axis.range * label.offset
           z.axis.y <- z.axis.y - axis.range * label.offset

           # Start making graph

           if ( !is.null(GraphSheet) && nchar( GraphSheet ) > 0)
                     graph.name <- paste(GraphSheet,"$1",sep="")
           else
                     graph.name <- ""

           guiCreate("Graph2D", Name=graph.name,
                               HorizontalShift = 2,
           VerticalShift = 0.95,
           DisplayWidth = 7,
           DisplayHeight = 7,
           Hide = F,
           xPlotOrigin = 0.7,
           yPlotOrigin = 0.920514,

           GraphBorderStyle = "None",
           GraphBorderColor = "Black",

# Create actual plot

piperplot <- function(x, y, z, use.labs=T, labs=seq(along=x), min=0,
max=100, tol=0.001,
           jitter=.03*max, orient="c", xlab="x", ylab="y", zlab="z") {

# Created by Sama Low Choy, 22 July 1998
# Draw a piper plot of three compositional variables x,y,z.
# Produces an equilateral triangle with each side running from
#     min to max. Points are placed within the triangle to
#     indicate how much of each component is present at that point.
# Axes are oriented "c"lockwise or "a"nticlockwise.

# Check that composition is completely specified
if (sum(x+y+z-max) > length(x)*tol)
           stop(message=paste("Components don't add up to",max))

# Compute midpoint of x and y/z axes
mid <- (max+min)/2
height <- sqrt(max^2 - mid^2)
qmid<- mid/2
qheight <- sqrt(mid^2 - qmid^2)

# plot axes
par(pty="s")
plot(c(min,mid,max), c(min,height,min), type="n", axes=F,xlab=xlab,ylab="")
lines(c(min,max,mid,min), c(min,min,height,min), type="l")

# set up labels on three axes
if (orient == "c")
           axis.labels <- c(max,mid,min)
else
           axis.labels <- c(min,mid,max)

# lower axis
text(x=c(min-jitter, mid, max+jitter), y=rep(min-jitter,3),
           labels=axis.labels)
lines(c(mid,mid),c(min-jitter*1/3,min+jitter*1/3),type="l")

# right axis
text(x=(c(min, qmid, mid)-jitter*sqrt(3)), y=(c(min,qheight,height)
+jitter),
           labels=rev(axis.labels), srt=60)
lines((qmid+c(-1,1)*jitter*sqrt(3)/6), (qheight+c(1,-1)*jitter/6),
           type="l")
text(x=qmid-jitter*3*sqrt(3), y=qheight+3*jitter, labels=ylab, srt=60)

# left axis
text(x=(c(mid, 3*qmid, max)+jitter*sqrt(3)), y=(c(height,qheight,min)
+jitter),
           labels=rev(axis.labels), srt=300)
lines((3*qmid + c(-1,1)*jitter*sqrt(3)/6), (qheight + c(-1,+1)*jitter/6),
           type="l")
text(x=3*qmid+jitter*3*sqrt(3), y=qheight+3*jitter, labels=zlab, srt=300)

# position points

if (orient == "c")
           x.triangle <- (z+max-x)/2
else
           x.triangle <- (x+max-z)/2

y.triangle <- sqrt(3)/2*y

# plot points
if (use.labs) {
           text(x.triangle,y.triangle,labels=labs,cex=0.5)
} else {
           points(x.triangle,y.triangle)
}

}

messages.body_plain:
I write and support S Plus functions for non-statisticians with mixed success.
   My clientele are primarily clinicians.  Mostly these are smart people who
   majored in biology instead of chemistry because they were afraid of math.
   They are not comfortable with anything that resembles programming.
   Many only use a function once or twice a month, which is not often enough for
   retention.
Nevertheless, sometimes it works.  The payback when it works is high - the
clients get faster turn around time and my department doesn't get bogged down
with repetitive work.

I am constrained to Microsoft Office 97.  Excel Macros are not adequate.  S Plus
is still too awkward for a casual user.  (For a counter example check out how
easy it is to import data from Excel to Minitab.  By the way, Minitab macros are
also inadequate.  I need a true programming language with flexible graphics
capability, i.e. S Plus)

Ideally things could be set up so that
*  the clinician enters the data into Excel using a prescribed format,
*  following a menu/window system the clinician enters the information needed to
run the function,
*  S Plus runs the function behind the scenes, and
*  the graphs show up in Word or Excel.

I have been told that this can all be done with Visual Basic.  Can anyone
recommend a good Visual Basic reference that covers the situation outlined
above?

I will summarize to the list.

Thank you so much for you input.
KJJ

warning messages but I have not been able to figure out how.  I had thought
the key was the object last.warning, but this is not visible within my
function.

messages.subject: [S] Weird behaviour of cbind.
messages.body_plain:
Hi S-users,

I have the following data.frame:

> class(ttt)
[1] "data.frame"
> dim(ttt)
[1] 39  4

> names(ttt)
[1] "Differentiel" "Value"        "Std. Error"   "t value"

Basically the output from builtin function summary.glm plus an extra column.
Now I want to "cbind" another column to ttt as follows:

> ttt.2_cbind(ttt,  c(NA, rep(0, dim(ttt)[1] - 1)))

> names(ttt.2)
[1] "Differentiel" "Value"        "Std..Error"   "t.value"      "X2"

Now where does the extra "." in Std..Error and the "." in t.value come from?

I find this disturbing, as a person can't know for sure what the column's names
will be.  If those names are used to pick some elements from some columns
afterwards a person can't rely on the names that S+ will assign to the
columns.  Yes I know, the blanks were replaced by ".", but why did the
developers gave column's names with blanks in them if other functions can't
handle them further down the road.

Any insights, anyone?

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 8 Mar 2000, George  Bagnall wrote:

[...]
> I am using trellis commands, supplied to me by Song Qian from Portland State
> University, to create a page of 9 graphs (see below).  The first column of
> three is cumulative distributions, the second qq plots, and the third tmd
> plots.  I need, however, to add a page title to the display in order for
> readers to make sense of the graphs.  I tried using mtext to add a title to
> the page but this did not work.  I ended up getting a page with a title on
> it and a separate page with the graphs.  I haven't been successful in

Whatever makes you think that you can use mtext with Trellis?  Trellis
is a separate way of doing graphics, and it takes over the device and
alters most of the graphics settings for its own purposes. In particular, 
as far as I recall it changes the settings of the outer margins.

The rule needs to be: use Trellis or traditional graphics (or GUI graphics) 
but don't expect to mix them until you are a master (and then you will not
want to).

The most obvious way to add a page title is to use main=, just as one would
in traditional graphics.

Trellis thinks of having multiple pages, and a way to getting labelling
precisely where you want it on each page is the page= argument. If you only
have one page, that should do the job too, and allows more control.

There is a Trellis manual: I have one dated 1996 from 3.4 (I think) and it
also used to be available online at AT&T (as was).  If you can find a copy,
it is helpful.

[...]

messages.subject: FW: [S] Splus5.1 vs 3.4
messages.body_plain:
In the mail below there is a reference to "null-string-attributes glitch".
What is that?

-----Original Message-----
From:   Beth Atkinson [mailto:atkinson at mayo.edu]
<mailto:[mailto:atkinson at mayo.edu]> 
Sent:   Monday, March 06, 2000 11:35 AM
To:     s-news at wubios.wustl.edu <mailto:s-news at wubios.wustl.edu> 
Subject:        [S] Splus5.1 vs 3.4

In my original post I asked what positive features/enhancements of Splus5.1
had people found.  Overall, the responses reinforced the notion that we'll
release 5.1 but the default will be 3.4.

The positives noted were -
*       compiling/loading externals is easier
*       It's available for Linux.
*       The latest rpart is only released for 5.1.
*       The functions bootstrap, multicomp, censorReg, importData, lmRobMM 
*       multiple comparisons after anova
*       more survival analysis capabilities 
*       We can import large objects using 5.1, and manipulate them, that are
impossible on 3.4.  Once the null-string-attributes glitch is known to
users, the speed is superior for large objects.
*       5.1 has a pdf graphics driver that is very handy.

        Thanks to everyone who replied:Patrick Connolly, Nicole DePriest,
Peter Perkins,  Brian D Ripley, B.Rowlingson, Todd Taylor, Steve Wofsy.

*       Beth Atkinson

        
****************************************************************************
**

*       Personally, I'd stick with 3.4 until they get some of the kinks
worked out of 5.1.
*       this is v5.1 on Irix6.x:

        my experience so far has not been so positive.  it seems to use more
memory (despite what the documentation claims), the help system stinks, and
there were a number of teethng problems (that StatSci-as usual- denied were
problems at all) with the actual installation.  and if it creates one more
MySwork directory (when i've asked it politely not to), i'm going to go
beserk.
        haven't found anything from the "what's new" stuff that has really
improved my life.  but it's still S and it still works.  oh, compiling and
loading externals is much easier.
*       The main ways 5.1 has affected me:

        1) It's slower for most things I do, especially Trellis graphics.
        2) It's more memory intensive for most things I do.
        3) It's available for Linux.
        The ever-advancing state of hardware has made (1) and (2) minor
considerations.
        Number (3) is the main benefit to me (and it's a big one).
        I've not yet availed myself of the new S4 features, but the improved
OOP model is probably a good thing.  I know the old one was certainly
difficult to work with.
        Migrating old functions and data has not been too hard.
*       I'd be very interested in what you find.  We haven't changed from
3.4 either, not being too keen on the debacle over the new class which could
have been done a whole lot better.  We have numerous functions accrued over
years, and it's quite useful knowing just how old they are.  If they have to
be redone, we lose the date information and with it any feeling of what our
competence was at the time it was written.  As yet, I've not noticed any
compelling reason to change, but you might find one.
*       The latest rpart is only released for 5.1?
        bootstrap, multicomp, censorReg (but maybe not if you want to keep
the boss happy), importData, lmRobMM, are ones I have used.
*       It's very hard to find stuff thats better in 5.1 than 3.4. Some of
my users report processes hogging even more memory in 5.1 than 3.4 - this
can be alleviated by rewriting loop code though, but its work. The help
system (now a java applet) has some major problems - first of course, you
need java enabled on your web browser (which currently crashes my netscape
installation 9 times out of 10, but thats probably my fault..), then there's
a few other minor complications if you are running Splus on a different box
to netscape.  Netscape wont necessarily find the help files, because Splus
might not even be installed on the machine running Netscape.

        Splus 5.1 incorporates the latest revision of the S language,
version
        4.      This causes plenty of headaches. Library code that used the
object oriented features of the previous version needs serious amounts of
rewriting. One of our locally developed libraries 'Oswald', was written
according to the old O-O system, and conforms to all the methods and dogma
laid down by that system. Yet porting it to Splus 5.1 hasnt happened yet,
since the automatic conversion tools that Splus 5.1 has dont work on it, and
hand crafting a conversion is a big task.  I've also been developing O-O
code for a different application from scratch, and that too is a nightmare.
I dont think many people are doing this - since a message I posted on S-news
about it a couple of weeks ago drew no response.  All I wanted to do was to
make a class that inherited from 'data.frame', but this seems impossible.

        Miscellaneous bugs in 3.4 have carried over to 5.1 - the irregular
image plot in postscript is still there (and this was reported in 1996 by
someone), and there are lots of problems with the Linux port. The Linux port
was the only reason we switched - since they dont do 3.4 for Linux. I've
recently reported a bug with signal handling in Splus 5.1 for linux. If you
interrupt (with Ctrl-C) an Splus function that does something like
unix("sleep 10") (or equivalently, sleep(10)), then Splus may crash - if not
at that point but at the next generated error!  I've also had random system
terminations due to address errors that I couldn't track down.
        Some of our lecturers are still having to use 3.4 because of library
code they havent converted to 5.1. This caused much embarrassment when I
taught all the students how to use 5.1 and then they have to be told to use
3.4, with all the hassle of switching between .Data for different
versions...
        Oh, I could go on....
*       multiple comparisons after anova

        more survival analysis capabilities
        The censorReg() function if any of your users need to fit models to
censored data (this is common in the environmental field, when analytical
labs report "non-detections", i.e., the best they can do is provide an upper
bound; I don't know if it happens with medical labs)
*       We can import large objects using 5.1, and manipulate them, that are
impossible on 3.4.  Once the null-string-attributes glitch is known to
users, the speed is superior for large objects.

        5.1     has a pdf graphics driver that is very handy.

The major negative is the unrliable export back to 3.4-type objects.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Rolf Turner, Andy Liaw, Samuel Buttrey, Nick Ellis and Pierre Joyet
for their comments on the use of cbind and data.frame, specifically on how those
functions deal with the names attribute.

Following you will find Samuel Buttrey's reply which pretty much reflects other
responders comments.

Thanks again

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat
télephone            : (418) 835-8839
télecopieur          : (418) 835-5865
courrier électronique: gerald.jean at spgdag.ca

"In God we trust all others must bring data"

---------------

Hi. There's an argument to cbind() and data.frame() to prevent this. In
general data.frame() will convert "illegal" names to "legal" ones...
> t1.data.frame <- data.frame ("Hi There"=1:5, "St. Louis"=6:10)
> t1.data.frame
  Hi.There St..Louis
1        1         6
2        2         7
3        3         8
4        4         9
5        5        10

(note the extra dots), but you can get around this with check.names=F.

> t2.data.frame <- data.frame ("Hi There"=1:5, "St. Louis"=6:10,
check.names=F)
> t2.data.frame
  Hi There St. Louis
1        1         6
2        2         7
3        3         8
4        4         9
5        5        10

When you cbind() or call data.frame, the names are converted...

> cbind (t2.data.frame, "Col3" = 1:5)
  Hi.There St..Louis Col3
1        1         6    1
2        2         7    2
3        3         8    3
4        4         9    4
5        5        10    5

...unless you set check.names=F again.

> cbind (t2.data.frame, "Col3" = 1:5, check.names=F)
  Hi There St. Louis Col3
1        1         6    1
2        2         7    2
3        3         8    3
4        4         9    4
5        5        10    5

I agree that giving "illegal" names was a poor design decision.

I hope this helps,
Sam Buttrey
