messages.subject: [S] Summary: predictions using lme() with corAR1()
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: predictions using lme() with corAR1()
messages.body_plain:
I would like to thank Jose Pinheiro and James Roger for their wonderful help
on this!!  Here's a summary (actually, it's a cutting and pasting) of their
replies.  I hope that in my cutting and pasting that I have not
misrepresented any of what was said.

Thanks again for everyone's help!!

-- Andy

The current version of the NLME library, 3.2, does 
not produce predictions that take into account the correlation
structure of the within-group errors, when an individual has been
previously observed. This is a topic in the "to do" list that will 
eventually be incorporated into the code, but not into the immediate
future. 

> My question is how does Phi get incorporated into a predictive equation?
> I've looked in the standard Splus sources and wasn't able to find an
answer.
> 
> My intuition tells me that I'd simply use an equation like:
> 
> yhat(t) = b0hat + b1hat*x1(t) + b2hat*x2(t) + b3hat*x1(t)*x2(t) + BLUP(i)
-
> 0.691*yhat(t-1)
> 
> Where "t" indexes the time (which is discrete).  Am I thinking of this
> correctly?  

Almost. The correlation structure applies to the within-group errors
and only indirectly to the responses, y_t. In the case of corAR1, the
model is

        e_t = phi * e_{t-1} + u_t

where the u_t are iid N(0, sig2). The prediction for a previously
observed individual has two components: one associated with the fixed
and random effects (what's currently returned by the predict function)
plus a prediction for the within-group error. The formula in your case
would be

yhat(t) = b0hat + b1hat*x1(t) + b2hat*x2(t) + b3hat*x1(t)*x2(t) + BLUP(i) -
    0.691*ehat(t-1)
        
where ehat(t-1) is the within-group residual at time t-1, given by 

 y(t-1) - (b0hat + b1hat*x1(t-1) + b2hat*x2(t-1) +
        b3hat*x1(t-1)*x2(t-1) + BLUP(i))

Note that ehat(t) can only be calculated as above for the observed
t. For forecasting, you could use ehat(t+1) = phi * ehat(t),
ehat(t+2) = phi^2 * ehat(t), and so on. 

Thus, for pointwise predictions for individuals not previously observed, the
Phi does not come into play (nor do the BLUPs). The idea behind the
predictions is that you are trying to get the conditional expectation of the
unobserved response given the observed data. If the new observation is
independent of the observed data, the best you can do is to use the marginal
expectation, which only depends on the fixed effects. However, the phi is
used in the derivation of prediction intervals for the new value (though we
have not yet implemented it in NLME), so it's important to get its
estimate.

messages.subject: RE: [S] S+ vs. SAS
messages.body_plain:
As a follow up to this post:

I would say it also depends on the nature of your
work- if you are modeling data using well established
methods and your data has character fields and needs
lots of cleaning, the SAS often works well with its
extensive capabilities from PROCS and SQL. 

However, if you are developing sophesticated models
that need to be written in Matrix Algebra, then SPLUS
beats SAS IML anyday. 

With SPLUS you can directly work on an element in the
matrix/object and loop through and switch directions
and do sub-loops and write conditioinal processing
much easier. For some of that work (even for
bootstrapping) SAS is really painful.
SPLUS has very good time series and smoothning
programs - SAS is still catching up here.

With SPLUS you can edit existing cide and write your
own algorithm - a definite plus for esoteric work...
and of course SPLUS graphics is better....

Rgds

--- Max_Kuhn at ms.bd.com wrote:
> 
> 
> 
> 
> From: Max Kuhn@BDX on 03/29/2000 04:23 PM
> 
> My beliefs are these:
> 
> Advantages of SAS:
> 
> It's better for rote calculation. From
> pharmaceutical trials, it's been my
> experience that some regulatory agencies will want
> to see the most basic
> analysis performed for every possible subgroup 
> (this opinion does not reflect
> the opinions of Dr. Kuhn's employers....). In this
> case, "By processing" will
> save your life. If you have to compute summary
> statistics for a large number of
> subjects and then for each clinically significant
> subgroup, it can be quite a
> task to do the calculations and organize them for
> everyone to easily process.
> 
> With version 7 and above, the ability to export
> results to html is very simple
> and appears to be robust. The ability to get results
> out of S+ in report ready
> formats, in my experience, are less mature than
> those in SAS are.
> 
> If any problems arise, SAS's technical support is
> timely and effective. On one
> occasion, within 5 minutes of sending an email to
> tech support, my phone rang
> with an answer. They we so efficient, it was spooky.
> If you are in the 30
> response for a submission and you can't figure out
> why X is happening, this is a
> blessing.
> 
> Advantages of S-Plus:
> 
> For many types of analyses, S-Plus will be better.
> In survival analysis they are
> about equal, but any type of smoothing,
> bootstrapping or robust regression will
> be simpler is S-Plus (there are other examples).
> 
> S-Plus graphics are superior. You can probably get
> SAS/Graph to do exactly the
> same thing, but it will take considerable more time
> and effort. I've never had
> problems exporting graphics in S-Plus and the
> selection of plots from the GUI is
> substantial. I would much rather click on an axis to
> change it than to re-run a
> portion of code after figuring out how to code it
> properly. However, if you are
> creating a large number of graphs that are very
> similar, S-Plus can get bogged
> down if you have too much open.
> 
> The bottom line:
> 
> You probably need both. It's not difficult to get
> data in and out of each. I
> have found that I need these two packages plus
> Minitab (for SPC) plus StatXact
> (for small sample studies) and so on, but I have a
> wide range of areas to work
> in. For strictly clinical trials, I would leverage
> the strengths of both.
> 
> Max
>

messages.subject: [S] Re: S Data storage and the filesystem
messages.subject_clean: [S] Re: S Data storage and the filesystem
messages.body_plain:
"Martinez, Jesus" wrote:

> The main problem i have found in using S-PLUS up to now is
> with understanding how S-PLUS manages the files.

This is not well explained and done differently from the way that most programs
do it.  Mathsoft apparently considers this an "advanced topic," while at least
you and I consider it basic information.  There is a chapter in the Programmer's
Guide that explains this.  It is called "Command Line Options."  For S-Plus
2000, the chapter number is 19.

> 1- Why there are data frames files that i can see them at the Object
> Browser but i can not in the Windows Explorer, or at least apparently.
> For example i did some trellis graph, i can see the files with the Windows
> explorer but not in the Browser page, why?

They are S-Plus objects, not files.

> 2- What are those folders that i can see in my "database" or directory
> at the Windows Explorer, as "_init", "_prev", "_Help", or files as "_1",
> "_5", "_sum4", etc.... but i don´t see them at the Object Browser.

They are the files in which those objects are stored, usually in a format unique
to S-Plus.

> 3.-Why, even having the working database selected at the position 1 at the
> Object Browser, when i do a graph, the program saves them at another
> database, one within the S-PLUS Program files directory, and then when
> i try to find these graph files to copy them to my working database, i
> can not find them. I can see them with the Windows Explorer but not
> with the Object Browser.

A graph may or may not be considered an S-Plus object by the implementors of
S-Plus, depending on the context.  This is not predictable.  But the place that
a graph will be saved will ordinarily be within your S_PROJ directory, not
within the S-Plus database directory.  (Refer to that chapter for more
information on S-PROJ.)

--

messages.subject: [S] Splus censorReg() and SAS proc lifereg do not agree
messages.subject_clean: [S] Splus censorReg() and SAS proc lifereg do not agree
messages.body_plain:
The Splus function censorReg() and the SAS lifereg can both be used 
to fit a distribution to censored data. I am comparing results and 
have found that they agree, except for the covariance matrix of the 
parameter estimates. The parameter estimates themselves, and the 
log-likelihood at the solution, agree.

The differences are, I think, too large to be attributed to 
differences in numerical approximation to curvature in the vicinity 
of the solution.

I am hoping that someone can explain the differences and either show 
me how to transform from one to the other, or else tell me which one 
is wrong. The documentation for both products provides the same 
description, i.e., "estimated covariance matrix of the parameter 
vector" (SAS) or "the final covariance matrix of the estimated 
coefficients" (Splus). I've tested a number of different datasets and 
distributions and found the same pattern of disagreement.

Thanks in advance for any help.
-Don

Here is an example, using dummy data. The data consists of one 
interval censored measurement 0 <= x <= 1 and four exact measurements 
having values 2, 3, 4, and 5.

----------------------------
The covariance matrices are:
----------------------------
Splus:
Covariance matrix of parameter estimates
             (Intercept)   Log(scale)
(Intercept)  0.478825033 -0.003257816
 Log(scale) -0.003257816  0.103273571

SAS:
    INTERCEP     _SCALE_
     0.47882    -0.00502
    -0.00502     0.24557

Note that the estimated variances of the intercept agree; it is the 
others that do not.

SAS and Splus code to generate the data and fit the model are below. 
(SAS v6.12, Splus v5.1)

----------
Splus code
----------
vhi <- 1:5
vlo <- c(0,2:5)
vup <- c(1,NA,NA,NA,NA)
vcode <- c(3,1,1,1,1)
vcens <- censor( vlo , vup, vcode)
cat('Data\n')
print(vcens)
cat('\n')
fit <- censorReg(vcens~1,dist='gaussian')
cat('Fit\n')
print(fit)
cat('\n')
cat('-2*log-likelihood',-2*fit$loglik[1],'\n')
cat('\n')
cat('Covariance matrix of parameter estimates\n')
print(fit$var)

----------
SAS code
----------
title 'test fit normal distribution with left censoring';
data tstdat;
    do vhi=1 to 5;
        vlo=vhi;
        if vhi=1 then vlo=0;
        output;
        end;
run;
proc print data=tstdat;
run;
proc lifereg data=tstdat outest=cvm covout;
    model (vlo,vhi) = /dist=normal;
run;
title2 'covariance matrix of parameter estimates';
proc print data=cvm;
    where _type_='COV';
    var intercep _scale_;
run;
title2 'full covout dataset';
proc print data= cvm;
run;

----------------------------------------------------
For reference, here is the full output from the little Splus program above.
----------------------------------------------------
Data

 [0, 1] 2 3 4 5

Fit
Call:
censorReg(formula = vcens ~ 1, distribution = "gaussian")

Distribution: Gaussian

Coefficients:
 (Intercept)
    2.916427

Dispersion (scale) = 1.542034
Log-likelihood: -9.301132

Observations: 5 Total; 1 Censored
Parameters Estimated: 2

-2*log-likelihood 18.6023

Covariance matrix of parameter estimates
             (Intercept)   Log(scale)
(Intercept)  0.478825033 -0.003257816
 Log(scale) -0.003257816  0.103273571
--------------------------------
Don MacQueen
Environmental Protection Dept.
Livermore, CA, USA
Lawrence Livermore National Lab

messages.subject: Re: [S] external language question
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 30 Mar 2000, Karl Young wrote:

> Sorry in advance for the strange question. I've got a huge program in a
> language called IDL (interactive data language) that I don't want to
> rewrite. I'd also like to perform classification (e.g. using CART) on some

CART is the trademark of a commercial program. Do you mean that or the
tree routines in S-PLUS?

> data that it generates and do some further processing in the IDL program
> after that. It'd be great to use S-PLUS to perfrom the CART analysis,
> i.e. it'd be nice if I didn't have to write the CART code in IDL (I guess 
> I'm starting to sound pretty lazy...). 

Not at all: writing tree routines and getting them right is a difficult
task (as AT&T found: the ones in S-PLUS were originally (ca 1993) pretty
buggy).

> Does anyone have any example code
> using external calls to S-PLUS (any language is ok; I was planing on
> having to write some C glue routines anyway). I couldn't find any examples
> re. how to do that (though I found some references, e.g. V and R, that I
> thought implied that this wasn't a silly thing to try to do). Thanks for
> any tips. 

You don't give us much to go on. What OS, for example?  What can IDL do
by way of external calls?

When we do this sort of thing from S-PLUS, e.g. to call XGobi, the
simplest idea is to write some data files, call the application via
a system call, then read the files generated by the application.  If IDL
can do that with S-PLUS as the application, this is the simplest way
and ought to suffice.

If you are working on Windows and IDL supports DCOM you can use that
to drive S-PLUS from inside IDL. (S-PLUS manuals use the older name of OLE
Automation.)  If you are on Unix you may be able to use CORBA with the
experimental S/CORBA interface written by Duncan Temple Lang.

An alternative idea is to use RPart. That used to have a standalone C
version and may still do so. If not, it would be fairly easy to inteface
its C code directly to an application that can call compiled C code.

--

messages.subject: [S] Time Series

Dear S-Plus users,

I want to generate a time series from
a nonlinear autoregressive model of
order 1, for example from the EXPAR(1)
model introduced by Ozaki and Oda (1978)

X_t = \theta_1 * X_{t-1} + \theta_2 * X_{t-1} *
exp(- X_{t-1}^2) + \epsilon_t.

I would like to use an elegant routine which would
avoid the use of "for" or "For" loops. There is some
cost in computation time by using these commands.

Thanks for all suggestions.

Jacques Zuber

messages.subject: [S] Regression with autocorrelation
messages.body_plain:
I have a series of about 4000 data sets with 8 - 40 points each. The data 
approximately fits the form

Y(i,j) = A(i) + B(i)*t(i,j) + C(i)*t(i,j)^2 + D(i)*t(i,j)^3 + Z(i,j)

i in 1:4000
j in 1:(8-40)

Z(i,j) is an AR(2) process w.r.t j

Z(i,j) =  rho1 * Z(i,j-1) + rho2 * Z(i,j-2) + e(i,j)

Var(e(i,j)) = CapSig
cor(e(i,j),e(k,l)) = 1 if i==k && j==l, 0 ow.

Note that the coefficients A,B,C,D are different between each dataset, whereas 
the coefficients rho1, and rho2 are constant for all datasets.

Does anybody have a suggestion on the best way to estimate the coefficients 
A,B,C,D,rho1,rho2 and CapSig?

I don't even know a good way to solve for the simpler case where there is only 
one dataset (as opposed to 4000). The case of one dataset is a "text book 
example", which I am familiar with in principle, but which I don't know how to 
efficiently code in S+. I would also be interested in the solution for a single 
dataset.

Thanks in Advance,

Clark Sims

messages.subject: [S] Unique rows in a dataframe
messages.body_plain:
I apologize for a question that I know to be a FAQ.

I have a data frame with 11 rows and 3 columns.  Three of the rows have the
exact same data.  I would like to get rid of these duplicates and return a
dataframe containing only the 8 unique rows.

Example:
> TDAT
   T1 T2       T3 
 1  A  1 11/15/99
 2  A  1 11/29/99
 3  A  2 11/15/99
 4  A  3 11/15/99
 5  B  1 11/15/99
 6  B  1 11/15/99 *
 7  B  1 11/15/99 *
 8  B  3 11/15/99
 9  C  2 11/15/99
10  C  2 11/15/99 *
11  C  3 11/15/99

*=duplicated

I can use aggregate.data.frame and it works fine for my example. 

aggregate.data.frame(TDAT[,1],TDAT,length)
  T1 T2       T3 x 
1  A  1 11/15/99 1
2  B  1 11/15/99 3
3  A  2 11/15/99 1
4  C  2 11/15/99 2
5  A  3 11/15/99 1
6  B  3 11/15/99 1
7  C  3 11/15/99 1
8  A  1 11/29/99 1

I haven't been as successful using the aggregate.data.frame soluation with a
very large dataframe (>200,000 rows).  Is there a more elegant (and more
efficient)solution?

Thanks,

Paul Bliese
Walter Reed Army Institute of Research
paul.bliese at na.amedd.army.mil

>

You can extract the code from the s_spec.h in the include directory (You must 
install the the developers add ins when you install S+, I think?!)

I have hacked the code for C++ on X86 machines as follows:

#ifndef FMANT_BITS
#define FMANT_BITS      0x7fffff
#define DMANTHI_BITS    0xfffff
#define FEXP_BITS          0x7f800000
#define DEXP_BITS          0x7ff00000
#define F_SIGN_BIT      0x80000000
#define D_SIGN_BIT      F_SIGN_BIT
#define L_SIGN_BIT      F_SIGN_BIT
#endif

inline int _is_nan( const float  *f)
{
   return (((*(long*)f) & FEXP_BITS  == FEXP_BITS) && ((*(long*)f) << 9));
}

inline int _is_nan( const double *d)
{
   return ((((long*)d)[1] & DEXP_BITS) == DEXP_BITS) && (((long*)d)[1]<<12 || 
((long*)d)[0]);
}

I don't have time to do the same for big endian machines, but it should be 
fairly obvious from the header files. 

HTH,

Clark

messages.subject_clean: [S]: Placing text in an empty panel in Trellis Graphics
messages.body_plain:
I am using S-Plus 4.5 Professional on Windows.  I am looking for command line 
language to add text within a panel display which is empty.

For example, suppose I ran an experiment with 2 factors, but not all 
combinations.  Say factor A has three levels (A1, A2, A3) and factor B has 3 
levels (B1, B2, B3), but the combinations run are

A2 B1
A1 B2
A2 B2
A1 B3
A2 B3
A3 B3

For aesthetic reasons, I want all 9 combinations to show in the display, but 
would like to add text in the panels for the non-used combinations.  Within 
each panel I am plotting (x,y) data points along with a fitted regression line 
and confidence bands.  For those panels with no (x,y) data points to plot, I 
want to display text such as "Condition Not Studied".  

I have tried something of the form:

xyplot(y~x|A*B,data=mydata,
   panel=function(x,y){
      ifelse(length(x)>0,panel.xyplot(x,y),text(.3,.5,'Condition Not Studied'))
   })

Apparently, the panel function is not called when the packet is empty.  Is 
there a way to add text to the empty panels?

Thanks.

James Pratt
Sonus Pharmaceuticals
jimp at sonuspharma.com
